title: India's SIP Machine Has Grown Tenfold in a Decade. Equity Mutual Fund Flows Just Hit a One-Year Low. What NRIs Should Read Into Both.
excerpt: Monthly SIP contributions surged from ₹3,189 crore to ₹30,954 crore in ten years even as foreign investors dumped a record $30 billion of Indian stocks in 2026.
body:
Two data points released this week tell a single story about Indian markets — and they point in opposite directions.

Monthly systematic investment plan contributions have grown nearly tenfold over the past decade, from ₹3,189 crore in May 2016 to ₹30,954 crore in May 2026, according to a new report by ValueMetrics. Outstanding SIP accounts crossed 10.47 crore, up over 15 per cent year on year. Through demonetisation, Covid-19, the Russia-Ukraine war and now the Iran conflict, India's retail investors have kept feeding the machine.

At the same time, equity mutual fund inflows plunged 40 per cent month on month in May to ₹229.08 billion — the lowest in a year — as the US-Iran war, crude at $100 a barrel and a rupee sliding toward ₹97 rattled confidence. Foreign investors sold $3.45 billion of Indian equities in May alone and have dumped a record $30 billion in 2026.

## The Two Stories in One Market

The divergence is structural, not contradictory. Lump-sum equity allocations are discretionary — investors can and do pull back when volatility spikes. SIPs, by design, are automatic, emotion-proof monthly deductions. Their resilience through crisis after crisis is not bravery. It is architecture.

"The lower inflows are due to extreme volatility in the markets as crude hovers around $100 a barrel, which has prompted near-term caution among investors," said Venkat Chalasani, CEO of the Association of Mutual Funds in India.

But the SIP story is the ballast. SIP inflows held steady at $3.25 billion in May, barely changed from April. India's mutual fund industry now manages ₹81.6 lakh crore in assets under management, and SIP assets alone account for ₹17.12 lakh crore — roughly 21 per cent of the total.

## The Foreign Exit, Quantified

Foreign institutional investors now hold just 14.7 per cent of Indian equities, a 14-year low. Domestic institutional investors, led by mutual funds fed largely by SIPs, hold 18.9 per cent — a record high. This role reversal, which has accelerated in 2026, has profound implications.

For the first time in modern Indian market history, domestic flows are structurally large enough to absorb sustained foreign selling. In April, foreign investors sold ₹60,847 crore while domestic institutions bought ₹51,064 crore. The market still went up.

India's benchmark Nifty 50 has fallen 10.6 per cent this year, but analysts argue the damage would have been far worse without the SIP cushion. BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, said last week that India has been "over-punished" and called it one of its highest-conviction medium-term emerging market trades.

## The Churn Problem Nobody Is Talking About

Beneath the tenfold growth headline, a less comfortable trend is emerging. In May, 54.2 lakh new SIP accounts were registered — but 51.7 lakh were discontinued or completed. Net new additions were just 2.5 lakh. In March and April, net additions had actually turned negative.

This churn — investors starting SIPs and stopping them within a year or two — is rising. Gross registrations at 5.2 per cent of outstanding accounts nearly match discontinuations at 5.0 per cent. If this gap narrows further, the SIP engine could stall even as absolute contribution numbers look healthy.

"A near-zero net addition signals that India's SIP growth is maturing," the ValueMetrics report noted. The question is whether the industry can re-accelerate penetration into Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities or whether SIP growth will plateau.

## What This Means for NRI Investors

For NRIs watching from abroad, the data offers three takeaways.

**One: India's domestic investor base is no longer a sideshow.** The days when foreign flows dictated market direction are fading. SIP-driven domestic capital now provides structural support that makes Indian equity less vulnerable to the kind of emerging-market capital flight that devastated it in 2013 or 2018.

**Two: Timing the market from overseas is getting harder.** Equity fund flows dropped 40 per cent in May, but SIPs were flat. The market's floor is now set by millions of monthly auto-debits, not by foreign risk appetite. NRIs who try to wait for a "safe" re-entry point may find that the floor keeps rising beneath them.

**Three: The FCNR deposit boom is a complementary play.** With Indian banks offering NRIs up to 7 per cent on dollar deposits — and the RBI absorbing the full hedging cost — there is now a low-risk route to park dollars in India while earning above US money-market rates. This is not either-or. Some NRIs are running SIPs for long-term equity exposure and FCNR deposits for short-term yield.

The Nifty is down. Foreign money is leaving. But India's retail machinery — built one ₹500-a-month SIP at a time — is holding the line. For NRIs deciding whether to stay invested, the architecture matters more than the headlines.

*Sources: Reuters, Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI), ValueMetrics, Reserve Bank of India*
